name: 1-proportion z-test
when: One group, a yes-or-no question, and a claim about the percent.
question: A company says 75% of its customers are happy. You survey 120 random customers and 84 of them (70%) are happy. Is the true percent lower than 75%?

steps.t: H₀: p = 0.75 and Hₐ: p < 0.75, where p is the true proportion of all customers who are happy. Use α = 0.05.
1-proportion z-test. Random: random sample ✓. 10%: 120 is less than 10% of all customers ✓. Large counts: np₀ = 90 and n(1 − p₀) = 30 are both at least 10 ✓.
0.10 is more than 0.05, so we fail to reject H₀. We don't have convincing evidence that fewer than 75% of all customers are happy.

name: 2-proportion z-test
when: Two groups, a yes-or-no question, and you want to compare their percents.
question: 300 students are randomly split into two groups of 150. One group gets a homework reminder text. 60 of them (40%) turn homework in on time, against 45 of the other group (30%). Does the text help?

steps.t: H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0 and Hₐ: p₁ − p₂ > 0, where p₁ and p₂ are the true on-time rates with and without the text. Use α = 0.05.

2-proportion z-test. Random: random assignment ✓ (the 10% check isn't needed for an experiment). Large counts: with the combined rate p̂c = 105 ÷ 300 = 0.35, the expected successes and failures (52.5 and 97.5 in each group) are all at least 10 ✓.
0.035 is less than 0.05, so we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence the reminder text raises the on-time rate. Because the groups were randomly assigned, we can say the text caused it.

name: Chi-square test for independence or homogeneity
when: Two category variables in a two-way table. Independence: one sample, two variables. Homogeneity: several groups, one variable.
question: A random sample of 300 students at a school records grade (9 to 12) and how they get to school (walk, bus or car). Are the two linked?

steps.t: H₀: grade and way of getting to school are independent for students at this school. Hₐ: they are not independent. Use α = 0.05.

χ² test for independence. Random: random sample ✓. 10%: the school has more than 3,000 students, so 300 is less than 10% ✓. Expected counts: (row total × column total) ÷ 300 for each cell, all at least 5 ✓.
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E over all 12 cells, with df = (4 − 1)(3 − 1) = 6. Say the calculator gives χ² = 21.4 and p-value ≈ 0.002.
0.002 is less than 0.05, so we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence that grade and the way students get to school are linked for students at this school.

name: 1-sample t-test for a mean
when: One group, a number you can average, and a claim about the mean.
question: The box says batteries last 10 hours. A random sample of 25 batteries lasts x̄ = 9.6 hours on average, with s = 1.0 hour. Is the true mean less than 10?

steps.t: H₀: μ = 10 and Hₐ: μ < 10, where μ is the true mean life of all these batteries. Use α = 0.05.
1-sample t-test. Random: random sample ✓. 10%: 25 is less than 10% of all batteries ✓. Normal: n = 25 is under 30, so check a graph of the sample: no strong skew or outliers ✓.
0.028 is less than 0.05, so we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence the true mean battery life is less than 10 hours.

name: Paired t-test (mean difference)
when: Two numbers from each person (like before and after). Subtract to get the differences, then test their mean.
question: 10 random students take a quiz, use a study app for a week, then retake it. The differences (after − before) have mean x̄d = 4.2 points and sd = 5.1. Do scores go up?

steps.t: H₀: μd = 0 and Hₐ: μd > 0, where μd is the true mean difference (after − before). Use α = 0.05.
Paired t-test. Random: random sample of students ✓. 10%: 10 is less than 10% of all students ✓. Normal: n = 10 is small, so a dotplot of the 10 differences should show no strong skew or outliers ✓.
0.014 is less than 0.05, so we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence that scores go up on average after the week. (There was no control group, so we can't be sure the app is what caused it.)

name: 2-sample t-test for means
when: Two separate groups, a number you can average, and you want to compare the means.
question: 70 students are randomly split: 35 study with music, 35 in silence. Music: x̄₁ = 78, s₁ = 10. Silence: x̄₂ = 83, s₂ = 9. Does music change the mean score?

steps.t: H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 and Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0, where μ₁ and μ₂ are the true mean scores with music and in silence. Use α = 0.05.
2-sample t-test. Random: random assignment ✓. Normal: each group has 35 students, which is at least 30 ✓.
t = (78 − 83) ÷ √(10²/35 + 9²/35) ≈ −2.20. The calculator gives df ≈ 67 and p-value ≈ 0.031.
0.031 is less than 0.05, so we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence that music changes mean scores (here it lowered them). Random assignment lets us say music caused the difference.
